question: According to the Maine CDL Manual, which combination is NOT allowed on Maine roads?
choice_a: Tractor-semitrailers
choice_b: Double trailers
choice_c: Triple trailers
choice_d: Straight trucks pulling a single trailer
explanation: The manual explicitly notes that the Doubles/Triples endorsement is for operation of double/triple trailers where allowed by law, and states plainly that triple trailers are not allowed in Maine.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, Maine Endorsement Note

question: Which trailer in a set of doubles is most likely to turn over because of the "crack-the-whip" effect?
choice_a: The last (rearmost) trailer
choice_b: The converter dolly itself
choice_c: Whichever trailer is empty, regardless of position
choice_d: The first trailer, directly behind the tractor
explanation: The manual states that doubles are more likely to turn over than other combination vehicles because of the crack-the-whip effect, and that the last trailer in a combination is most likely to turn over.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.1.2 Beware of the Crack-the-whip Effect

question: What must you do to prevent trailers from rolling over when pulling doubles?
choice_a: Steer gently and go slowly around corners, on ramps, off ramps, and curves
choice_b: Brake hard and steer sharply to reduce the crack-the-whip effect
choice_c: Accelerate through curves to maintain momentum
choice_d: Keep both hands loosely on the wheel to allow the trailers to self-correct
explanation: The manual states that to prevent trailers from rolling over, you must steer gently and go slowly around corners, on ramps, off ramps, and curves.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.1.1 Prevent Trailer from Rolling Over

question: Why should you allow more following distance when pulling doubles compared to a single-trailer combination?
choice_a: Doubles are longer and cannot be turned or stopped suddenly, so more space is needed
choice_b: Following distance is unrelated to trailer length
choice_c: Doubles have weaker brakes than single trailers
choice_d: State law requires an extra 500 feet of following distance for any multi-trailer combination
explanation: The manual explains that doubles take up more space than other commercial vehicles because they are longer and can't be turned or stopped suddenly, so more following distance and larger gaps are needed.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.1.5 Manage Space

question: Why must you be especially careful driving double trailers in bad weather or on slippery roads?
choice_a: You have greater length and more dead axles to pull with your drive axles, increasing the chance of skids and loss of traction
choice_b: Doubles have no ABS at all, regardless of manufacture date
choice_c: Doubles are exempt from standard air brake requirements
choice_d: The tractor protection valve is disabled in bad weather
explanation: The manual states that with double (and, generically, triple) bottoms you have greater length and more dead axles to pull with your drive axles, creating more chance for skids and loss of traction in adverse conditions.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.1.6 Adverse Conditions

question: What special concern should a driver of doubles keep in mind when choosing a parking spot?
choice_a: Only converter dollies require special parking consideration
choice_b: Make sure you do not get into a spot you cannot pull straight through, since backing a long combination is difficult
choice_c: Doubles may park in any spot sized for a single-trailer rig
choice_d: Always park facing downhill to make departure easier
explanation: The manual warns that you need to be aware of how parking lots are arranged in order to avoid a long and difficult escape, and to avoid a spot you cannot pull straight through.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.1.7 Parking the Vehicle

topic: Doubles and Triples - Converter Dolly ABS
question: Converter dollies built on or after what date are required to have antilock brakes?
choice_a: March 1, 1998
choice_b: March 1, 1990
choice_c: July 1, 2005
choice_d: January 1, 1975
explanation: The manual states converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have antilock brakes and will have a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.1.8 Antilock Braking Systems on Converter Dollies

question: What is a converter dolly?
choice_a: A backup air compressor mounted on the trailer frame
choice_b: A hydraulic jack used only to raise the landing gear
choice_c: A coupling device of one or two axles and a fifth wheel used to couple a semitrailer to the rear of a tractor-trailer, forming a double-bottom rig
choice_d: A type of glad hand used exclusively on tanker trailers
explanation: The manual defines a converter dolly (converter gear) as a coupling device of one or two axles and a fifth wheel by which a semitrailer can be coupled to the rear of a tractor-trailer combination, forming a double-bottom rig.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: For the safest handling on the road when pulling doubles, where should the more heavily loaded semitrailer be positioned?
choice_a: In the first position, directly behind the tractor
choice_b: Split evenly, since Maine requires equal axle loads on both trailers
choice_c: In the rear position, behind the converter dolly
choice_d: It makes no difference to handling
explanation: The manual states that for the safest handling on the road, the more heavily loaded semitrailer should be in first position behind the tractor, with the lighter trailer in the rear.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: How can you set the emergency brakes on a second (rear) trailer that lacks spring brakes before coupling?
choice_a: Apply the tractor's parking brake only
choice_b: Leave the emergency line disconnected the entire time to keep the brakes locked
choice_c: Pump the trailer hand valve rapidly ten times
choice_d: Connect the emergency line, charge the trailer air tank, then disconnect the emergency line
explanation: The manual explains that if the second trailer doesn't have spring brakes, you connect the emergency line, charge the trailer air tank, and then disconnect the emergency line, which sets the trailer emergency brakes.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: Before backing the converter dolly under the rear trailer, the trailer height must be:
choice_a: Irrelevant, since the dolly automatically adjusts height
choice_b: Exactly level with the tractor frame
choice_c: Set as high as possible to avoid dragging the dolly tongue
choice_d: Slightly lower than the center of the fifth wheel, so the trailer is raised slightly when the dolly is pushed under
explanation: The manual states the trailer height must be slightly lower than the center of the fifth wheel, so the trailer is raised slightly when the dolly is pushed under it.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: After connecting the converter dolly to the rear trailer, how do you test that the coupling is secure?
choice_a: Release all the trailer brakes and let the rig roll a few feet
choice_b: Pull against the pin of the second semitrailer and make a visual check for no space between the upper and lower fifth wheel
choice_c: Only check that the electrical cord is plugged in
choice_d: Drive at normal highway speed and observe trailer sway
explanation: The manual instructs testing the coupling by pulling against the pin of the second semitrailer and making a visual check -- no space between the upper and lower fifth wheel, with locking jaws closed on the kingpin.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: Why should you never unlock the pintle hook while the converter dolly is still under the rear trailer?
choice_a: The dolly tow bar may fly up, causing injury and making it very difficult to re-couple
choice_b: It will cause the tractor protection valve to fail permanently
choice_c: It automatically triggers the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_d: It is only a concern for triple-trailer rigs, not doubles
explanation: The manual explicitly warns to never unlock the pintle hook with the dolly still under the rear trailer, because the dolly tow bar may fly up, possibly causing injury and making re-coupling very difficult.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.2.2 Uncoupling Twin Trailers

question: When inspecting a set of doubles, how should the shut-off valves at the rear of the front trailer(s) be positioned?
choice_a: Open
choice_b: Half-open
choice_c: Closed
choice_d: Removed entirely
explanation: The manual states that shut-off valves at the rear of front trailers should be OPEN, while the shut-off valves at the rear of the last trailer must be CLOSED.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.3.1 Additional Checks

question: During inspection of a set of doubles, the converter dolly's air tank drain valve should be:
choice_a: Open
choice_b: Closed
choice_c: Set to the "emergency" position
choice_d: Removed for cleaning
explanation: The manual's double/triple trailer inspection checklist specifies that the converter dolly air tank drain valve should be CLOSED.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.3.1 Additional Checks

question: During a walkaround inspection of a set of doubles, what should you check regarding the pintle hook?
choice_a: Only that it is painted a visible color
choice_b: That the pintle-eye of the dolly is in place in the pintle hook and that the pintle hook is latched
choice_c: That it has been replaced within the last year
choice_d: Nothing; the pintle hook is not part of the required inspection
explanation: The manual's checklist for doubles/triples specifies making sure the pintle-eye of the dolly is in place in the pintle hook and that the pintle hook is latched.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.3.1 Additional Checks

topic: Doubles and Triples - Air Brake Check
question: When checking that air flows to all trailers on a set of doubles, what should you hear when you open the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer?
choice_a: Air escaping, showing the entire system is charged
choice_b: The ABS malfunction lamp beeping
choice_c: Complete silence, confirming no leaks anywhere
choice_d: A clicking sound from the tractor protection valve only
explanation: The manual describes opening the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer; you should hear air escaping, showing the entire system is charged.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks

topic: Doubles and Triples - Air Brake Check
question: If you do NOT hear air escaping from the service and emergency lines during the air-flow check on a set of doubles, what should you check first?
choice_a: That the tractor's engine oil level is correct
choice_b: That the ABS malfunction lamp bulb is not burned out
choice_c: That the trailer is within its legal weight limit
choice_d: That the shut-off valves on the trailer(s) and dolly(ies) are in the OPEN position
explanation: The manual instructs that if you do not hear air escaping from both lines, check that the shut-off valves on the trailer(s) and dolly(ies) are in the OPEN position, since air must reach all the way to the back for the brakes to work.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks

topic: Doubles and Triples - Air Brake Check
question: On a set of doubles, the tractor protection valve should pop out to the emergency position when air pressure falls into approximately what range?
choice_a: 20 to 45 psi
choice_b: 60 to 90 psi
choice_c: 5 to 10 psi
choice_d: 100 to 130 psi
explanation: The manual states the trailer air supply control should pop out (go to emergency) when air pressure falls into the range specified by the manufacturer, usually 20 to 45 psi -- the same check applies to doubles as to other combination vehicles.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.4.1 Additional Air Brake Checks

topic: Doubles and Triples - Look Far Ahead
question: Why should a driver pulling doubles look far ahead down the road?
choice_a: So you can slow down or change lanes gradually, avoiding rollover or jackknife from sudden maneuvers
choice_b: It is only necessary to spot police checkpoints
choice_c: To count the number of trailers in oncoming traffic
choice_d: Looking far ahead has no safety benefit for doubles specifically
explanation: The manual states that doubles must be driven very smoothly to avoid rollover or jackknife, so you should look far ahead to slow down or change lanes gradually when necessary.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.1.4 Look Far Ahead

topic: Doubles and Triples - Coupling Twin Trailers
question: According to the manual, if the distance is not too great, how can you position a converter dolly in front of the second trailer?
choice_a: It can never be moved by hand under any circumstances
choice_b: Wheel the dolly into position by hand so it is in line with the kingpin
choice_c: Push it with a forklift only
choice_d: Tow it behind a passenger vehicle
explanation: The manual states that if the distance is not too great, you can wheel the dolly into position by hand so it is in line with the kingpin, or use the tractor and first semitrailer to pick it up.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.2.1 Coupling Twin Trailers

question: When uncoupling the rear trailer of a set of doubles, what should you do before pulling the dolly out from under it?
choice_a: Fully disconnect the tractor from the first trailer
choice_b: Lower the landing gear of the second semitrailer enough to remove some weight from the dolly
choice_c: Remove the spare tire from the converter dolly
choice_d: Disable the ABS system on the rear trailer
explanation: The manual's uncoupling procedure for twin trailers includes lowering the landing gear of the second semitrailer enough to remove some weight from the dolly before pulling the dolly out.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.2.2 Uncoupling Twin Trailers

question: A Maine CDL applicant studying the AAMVA base manual sees generic instructions for coupling and uncoupling a triple-trailer rig. What should the applicant understand about applying this on Maine roads?
choice_a: Triples are allowed in Maine only at night
choice_b: Triples are allowed in Maine only with a hazardous materials endorsement
choice_c: Maine requires the exact same procedure and allows triples on all interstate highways
choice_d: The procedure is standard AAMVA content, but triple trailers are not allowed to be operated in Maine
explanation: The Maine manual's Doubles/Triples endorsement note clarifies the endorsement covers double/triple trailers 'where allowed by law' and explicitly states triple trailers are not allowed in Maine, even though the base AAMVA content describes generic triple-trailer procedures.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, Maine Endorsement Note

topic: Doubles and Triples - Sliding Fifth Wheel Inspection
question: When inspecting the sliding fifth wheel on a set of doubles, what should you verify about the locking pins?
choice_a: All locking pins are present and locked in place
choice_b: Only one locking pin is required regardless of design
choice_c: Locking pins should be removed before highway driving
choice_d: Locking pins are optional if the slide is greased
explanation: The manual's sliding fifth wheel checklist for doubles/triples requires checking that all locking pins are present and locked in place.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.3.1 Additional Checks

question: During inspection of a set of doubles, what should you verify about the light cords between trailers?
choice_a: They are firmly in the sockets on the trailers
choice_b: They only need to be checked on the lead trailer
choice_c: They are disconnected until the rig reaches highway speed
choice_d: They should be wrapped in tape regardless of connection status
explanation: The manual's doubles/triples inspection checklist specifies making sure light cords are firmly in sockets on the trailers.
source_note: Maine Commercial Driver License Manual (2005 CDL Testing System base AAMVA content, Maine revision 7/24), Maine Secretary of State / Bureau of Motor Vehicles -- Section 7, Doubles and Triples, 7.3.1 Additional Checks
